submission.natural_language_explanation: L1/N682- is a retrospective lexical-register detector: it fires on the token that carries the lexical content of a word from informational written prose (news, legal, academic, documentation), both when that word is one token (' source', ' evidence', ' decision', ' penalty', ' research', ' analysis', ' testimony', ' policy', ' trial') and, when the word is split across pieces, on its completing final piece ('ury' in All-Century, 'alty' in Penalty, 'icular' in vehicular, ' Degree' in First Degree). In the same grammatical slot it is near zero on everyday conversational/domestic vocabulary (' weather', ' island', ' church', ' wife', ' father', ' umbrella', ' kettle', ' carpet', ' version', ' attention'), on personal names, and on the first/middle pieces of the same multi-token words (mean strength 0.025 vs 0.010, and 12.0% vs 2.9% above the active threshold); the response is graded, not categorical, and it does not prepare any particular next token.

The forecast for the bank holiday had been wrong all week, and by Friday I had stopped checking it. My sister rang on Thursday evening to say she was driving up for the weekend with the kids, which meant the spare room had to be cleared out and the air bed dragged down from the loft. I spent most of Friday shifting boxes and bags of old clothes into the garage, and by the evening the room looked almost like a room again, with a lamp sitting on a crate and a chair wedged between the wall and the bed. The loft ladder is broken, so getting anything down from up there involves standing on a chair and hoping for the best, which is how I ended up on the floor with a mouthful of dust and a box of decorations on my head.

On Saturday we drove out to the coast because the forecast promised sun, and for once the forecast was right. The car park was nearly full, so we left the car on the grass verge and walked the last half mile along the cliff path, which was muddy and busy with people walking small dogs. My sister had brought a flask of tea and a bag of slightly squashed sandwiches, and we sat on a bench looking down at the water while the wind tried to take the paper cups out of our hands. The kids ran ahead to the arcade and came back with pockets full of two-pence coins and a plastic spider each, and we told them we were not putting any more money in the machines, and then of course we did.

By the time we got back to the house everyone was too tired to cook, so we ordered chips and ate them out of the paper on the kitchen floor because the table was still covered in boxes. We cleared the table eventually and put the boxes in the garage, and then we sat in the front room with the windows open because it was still warm. The kids made a fort out of the cushions and would not go up to bed until my sister threatened to take the television away, which she does about once a month and has never actually done.

On Sunday it rained, so we stayed inside. The kids watched the same cartoon three times, and at some point the smallest one fell asleep sitting up with a biscuit in his hand, which was somehow the best part of the whole weekend. After lunch my sister showed me something on her phone about sleep and screens. She said the research on teenagers and phones was the one thing that had finally convinced her to put her own phone in a drawer after nine, and that she had been sleeping better than she had in years. I said I would try it, and she said I would not, and we both knew she was probably right.

They left on Monday morning in a rush, with one shoe missing and a bag of wet swimming things in the boot, and the house went quiet in that strange way it does after everyone has gone. I made a cup of tea and stood in the kitchen for a while looking at the pile of bedding by the door, and then I went back to bed myself for an hour, which I have not done on a Monday in a very long time.
